Basic economic theory applies to minimum wage as much as any other product. No minimum wage should lead to natural unemployment (AKA, the unemployment rate of people between two jobs). Since unemployment is only measured based on people actively searching for jobs, it's a pretty shit measure, but no minimum wage would mean a job for everyone who needs one (the particularly rich would have no reason to work, of course). Skilled and educated workers would still fetch a decent wage, since firms would still have to compete over them, but hiring unskilled workers wouldn't need to be as much of a drain on resources.

Unlike most Western populations, these guys don't need massive houses, property, et cetera just to themselves to live with a little dignity, so they'd be more than happy with those jobs. There'd also be the issue of monopoly, and personal relationship discrimination, like in any other economic sector. A firm with an employment monopoly over a region would choose the wage itself, instead of having the wage be determined by the market equilibrium as it should be, which would lead to those areas becoming poor, then uneducated, then unskilled until they are no longer a decent workforce. Relationship discrimination, which is the #1 form of discrimination in hiring, would potentially also become a more massive circlejerk, by making it easy to pay someone you like much more than someone you don't. I'm sure I don't need to go into any more detail for anyone to see how horrible or dangerous any of these are, but I still agree with lower-than-equilibrium minimum wages (where basically everyone would get paid more than minimum wage) except in unique circumstances such as monopolies.

Many of the arguments being made in this thread are micro-economic arguments from the perspective of a single small business owner. Let's add a little macroeconomic perspective.

Small businesses make up: 99.7 percent of U.S. employer firms, 64 percent of net new private-sector jobs, 49.2 percent of private-sector employment, 42.9 percent of private-sector payroll, 46 percent of private-sector output, 43 percent of high-tech employment, 98 percent of firms exporting goods, and 33 percent of exporting value. Source: U.S. Census Bureau, SUSB, CPS;

This data is a little old but it gives us a decent picture. With the increasing market shares of big box retailers and the struggles that small business owners face, these numbers are probably a little higher than they would be today. However, the question needs to be asked, "what percentage of small business employees are making minimum or near minimum wages?" I can't find a figure, but I suspect that the vast majority of minimum wage workers are working at Wal Marts and McDonalds restaurants, etc (which are not small businesses, a franchisee may be running a small business, and their margin may be thin, but they buy literally everything from corporately contracted suppliers, who could cut franchisees a break on materials and take a cut in profits--of which they pocket the majority).

And furthermore, the impact that the increase in wages paid might have needs to be weighed against the benefits to the entire economy that comes with higher wages. If the minimum wage is higher, the average worker has more money to spend, and feels less inclined to save what they have because they have greater existential security. This benefits all businesses, but especially small business who lose market share more quickly and more dramatically when disposable income in the economy is low than do large corporations. Many small business owners realize this.

Ultimately, when wealth becomes too concentrated every business sees falling demand. A robust market depends on widespread prosperity to drive demand, which creates jobs, which raises disposable income, which creates demand, which creates jobs, etc. This can either be accomplished through the market (by forcing an increase in wages--something it should be noted that businesses could do willingly, but don't), or post-market through taxation and wealth redistribution.

A better solution might be to change the legal foundations upon which the market functions, and through which the distribution of income is shaped (property rights, contract laws, bankruptcy laws, patent/trademark/copyright laws, etc). These things have been systematically re-calibrated over the last four decades in the U.S. in ways that work to enshrine wealth and extend the market shares of large corporations. These effects are hard to notice because they are hidden within the market, and the rhetoric of the invisible hand pretends these are natural market forces, unmolested by the legal foundations of the market (which is silly).

However you want to approach the problem, it is a problem, and the alternative to addressing the problem is a collapse of the economy under the weight of the opulent.

but in defence of what phones actually do with fingerprint sensing now, (and Laptops I guess), is that they place the image into a vector template and produce an algorithm which can reproduce the fingerprint.

then this algorithm is hashed and stored.. each time you press your finger on the sensor the CPU has to re-determine the algorithm that is used to figure out the fingerprint. (actually, in the case of apple they store 5 differing algorithms and 3 have to match)

I couldn't say for sure, but you can always read up on How Capacitive Sensors work

You don't need an actual finger. Capacitive sensors only look for a change in the circuts capacitance (Ability to store a charge). By adding the human body to a circuit (When you touch the sensor) the capacitance goes up, the sensor sees this change, and trips the logic that tells the system that something as touched it. Some high end systems might look for specific ranges.

In order to defeat this you just need something that will allow electrons to flow. It turns out, researchers have found that gummy bears (And other things) work perfectly to provide a pathway for the sensor. All the attacker has to do is create a fake thumb print on a finger tip made from melted down gummy bears and the system will see the combined capacitance of the fake finger tip (negligible) and the attacker.

It's frequently been shown that finger print readers are trivial to defeat

While matching multiple algorithms may be handy if the attacker only has a partial finger print, once the whole finger print is acquired you have enough to fool the reader. Fingerprints can be lifted from anywhere since we constantly touch things in the world around us, and have even been recovered from photos.

Bypassing the capacitive sensor has been shown to be trivial at best. Because each person will have a different capacitance based on body mass, moisture content in the skin, and other factors, the only thing it's looking for is that there is some capacitance (Higher end sensors might restrict this to a specific range). Apparently gummy bears make for a perfect thumb replacement as they conduct the capacitance onto the attackers body. Some high end systems also have heat sensors to detect body heat, but this suffers from the same issues as the capacitave sensors.
